 D.C. Lawmakers Are Uneasy With Possible $25 Minimum Wage Vote Next Year
 An initiative that would increase the city’s minimum wage is likely to appear on the ballot in April.
 A wide range of D.C. Council members are speaking out against Initiative 87. (Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP)
 By Martin Austermuhle 
 November 19, 2026 
 05:25 a.m. 
 Email
 LinkedIn 
 Twitter 
 Copy 
 Link copied 
 It was a decade ago that progressive activists threatened to put a measure on the D.C. ballot calling for the city’s minimum wage — then $10.50 — to increase to $15 an hour . D.C. lawmakers saw the writing on the wall, and preempted them by unanimously passing a bill doing just that.
 Those same groups are at it again, but now they want the minimum wage — currently $18.40 — to jump to $25 .
 This time, though, many local legislators are either skeptical or outright opposed.
 A wide range of D.C. Council members — including progressive stalwarts and the mayor-elect — are speaking out against Initiative 87, the wage-hiking ballot measure that is likely to be put to voters next April. On top of increasing the minimum wage to $25 an hour by 2029, it would also fully phase out the tipped wage paid to restaurant workers by two years after that.

 Many lawmakers tell The Washington Sun that the jump in pay would be too much for local businesses, especially amidst a broader faltering of the city’s economy in the wake of widespread federal layoffs.
 “I totally understand why we would want to increase the minimum wage, but I don’t believe the time is right for this type of measure,” said Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker. “Many of our businesses are barely hanging on, and not only would this undercut the momentum that some are finally seeing, but it would send the wrong message to new businesses.”
 “For the small businesses I hear from that are really struggling to pay the rent, I don’t see how that’s the right option,” added Ward 6 council member Charles Allen.
 Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George has taken a similar position, telling The Sun earlier this year that moving to a $25 minimum wage “is not something that is practical and feasible right now.” That also goes for Ward 1 council member-elect Aparna Raj — like Lewis George, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America — who told WAMU 88.5 that while she supports a $25 minimum wage, she has questions about the timeline the initiative would impose.
 “I want to work with those small businesses around implementation and making sure we have a timeline that’s sustainable for them and workers as well,” she said. “I share concerns about the timeline on the initiative and want to amend that so it’s sustainable but that we can move towards that $25 minimum wage.”
 The ballot initiative is backed by New York-based advocacy group One Fair Wage, which has helped spearhead a national push for increasing the minimum wage to at least $25. The group says that minimum wages should reflect the actual cost people incur to live where they do; in D.C., that “living” wage would be more than $26 an hour, according to the MIT Living Wage Calculator .
 Saru Jayaraman, the president of One Fair Wage, has told The Sun that Americans are more concerned than ever with affordability, and she rejects the arguments that increasing wages would negatively impact local businesses or the city’s economy.
 “What happens when they get more money in their pockets, working people? They don’t put it in a 401(k),” she said. “It doesn’t go to the Cayman Islands or a Swiss bank account. They spend it in the economy. That is how small businesses are growing faster in higher-wage states. That’s how it’s happened every single time the minimum wage has gone up.”
 Even some skeptics of Initiative 87 agree with one of its underlying points: D.C. has become unaffordable for many residents.
 “We want to be able to keep people in D.C., and that requires making it easier for them to be able to pay their rent, their utilities, their groceries,” said Raj. “That’s not only lowering the cost of goods, that is also making it easier for workers to afford that with higher wages.”
 Still, D.C. has lost tens of thousands of federal government jobs over the last 18 months, the city faces a growing budget deficit next year, investment in the housing market has slowed significantly and officials concede the city has to do more to transform itself to be less reliant on the federal government and more friendly to small businesses.
 Lewis George said she wants to focus on making the city more affordable by bringing down the costs of utilities, housing and child care, instead of just increasing the city’s minimum wage. And At-Large council member-elect Oye Owolewa says he agrees that there needs to be a balance struck between what it costs to live in D.C. and what it costs to run a business in the city.
 “D.C. is at a turning point,” Owolewa said. “Growing our economy and raising wages over the next five to 10 years should be the whole District’s goal, and that means building an economy that doesn’t lean on a few industries. Restaurants, hotels and service businesses should not carry the cost of higher wages alone.”
 An underlying factor driving some of the opposition to Initiative 87 from the Wilson Building is the fact that the wage hike would come via a ballot initiative — and one decided in a likely low-turnout special election — instead of through the regular legislative process. (The tipped wage has been the subject of two ballot initiatives over the last decade, in 2018 and 2022.)
 “I have concerns with doing this type of policy by initiative,” said At-Large council member Elissa Silverman, who also worries that Initiative 87 would lead to “tremendous job loss.”
 Silverman tells The Sun she is considering introducing legislation to change how D.C.’s ballot initiative process works, potentially by tweaking it so it’s an indirect initiative like in Massachusetts , where voters can propose ideas directly to legislators — and it only goes back on a statewide ballot if those legislators choose not to act on it at all.
 A campaign led by the D.C. restaurant industry has been launched to urge residents to vote against Initiative 87 in April. At the same time, One Fair Wage and its supporters — including Andy Shallal, the owner of the D.C.-born chain Busboys and Poets — are pushing forward with the initiative, as well as bills in Congress that would increase the federal minimum wage to $25.
 On Wednesday they highlighted a national poll they say shows widespread national support for a higher minimum wage: 71% of respondents said it’s important for Congress to move toward the $25 living wage.
 The D.C. Board of Elections is expected to determine in early December whether proponents of Initiative 87 submitted enough signatures to place the measure on the ballot for the planned special election set for Apr. 6, 2027.
 Author
 Martin Austermuhle 
 is a reporter at The Washington Sun.
